summary.text: 日 is a picture of the sun. Shang-period sources also report uses for daylight and as a unit of days, but do not establish which use came first.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts the sun. Early forms could be rounded or squared, and a central mark is described as distinguishing 日 from 囗. The later Shuowen analysis divides it into 囗 and 一, but earlier evidence does not establish those as original components.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples document 日 in early inscriptional traditions. The sources report oracle-bone uses for the sun, daylight, and a day unit, but do not verify the dates of the individual inscriptions. The documented script categories include oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript, and seal forms; the evidence does not date every form or establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes.

The received Han-era Shuowen account analyzes 日 as 从囗一, interpreting the outline as the sun and the inner stroke as its undiminished center. This is a later explanation, not direct evidence for the graph's earliest structure.

uncertainties.text: Shang-period inscriptions attest uses for the sun, daylight, a five-day period, and a sacrificial name. Their relative order and semantic connections are not established; exact dates for individual inscriptions are also unresolved.
The evidence does not establish how each detail of the early graph formed or provide a dated sequence for its rounded and squared forms and central mark.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples attest 日 for the sun, and present-day Chinese dictionaries list this sense. Its use in the earliest documented corpus cited here does not prove it was the graph's first-ever use.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples use 日 for daylight, including in contrast with evening, and a present-day Chinese dictionary lists daytime as a sense. The evidence does not establish whether this use developed from the sun sense.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
senses.text: An oracle-bone example attests 日 for a five-day period, and present-day Chinese dictionaries list day as a calendrical unit. The evidence does not establish when or how this use relates to the sun and daylight uses.
The cited corpus includes 日 as a sacrificial name. Its relation, if any, to the sun, daylight, or day-unit uses is not established.

senses.period: current Chinese use; origin date unresolved
senses.text: Present-day Chinese dictionaries list 日 as an abbreviation for Japan, with examples such as 日貨 and 中日條約. The evidence does not establish when this abbreviation originated.

limitations.text: The inscriptions document several Shang-period uses but do not establish their relative chronology or transitions. Their shared early attestation does not show that one sense developed from another.

Modern readings and dictionary glosses alone do not establish a chronology or semantic path for later uses. Present-day Chinese dictionaries also record 日 as an abbreviation for Japan, but the evidence does not date its origin.

items.caption: This 日 redraw has a broadly rounded, irregular outline enclosing a filled oval. The image shows the attributed bronze-script form, but does not establish how the earliest graph was formed or what the inner mark meant.
items.alt: A thick, uneven oval-shaped black outline surrounds a smaller filled black oval.
items.selection_reason: The outline and central mark make this form useful for illustrating 日 as a sun pictogram. It is a modern redraw attributed to a mid-Western Zhou bronze form; the image-to-inscription match and the mark’s function are not verified by the drawing itself.
